desc:
You hold the number start and want to turn it into target. Three operations are available, with prices given by costs = [add, dbl, half]:

  • x -> x + 1 costs add;
  • x -> 2 * x costs dbl;
  • x -> x / 2, allowed only when x is even, costs half.

The number must always stay between 0 and limit inclusive, so an operation that would leave that range is not allowed. Return the minimum total price of a sequence of operations that turns start into target, or -1 if it is impossible. If start == target the price is 0.

start = 3, target = 10, limit = 40, costs = [4, 3, 1]
3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 10 costs 4 + 4 + 3 = 11
doubling first is dearer: 3 -> 6 -> 7 -> 8 -> 9 -> 10 costs 3 + 4*4 = 19
-> 11
hints: Think of every number from 0 to limit as a vertex, and every allowed operation as a directed edge with its price as weight.
The graph is implicit: you never need to build it, only generate the (at most three) neighbours of a number when you pop it.

Run Dijkstra from start. Neighbours of x are x + 1 (if at most limit), 2x (if at most limit) and x / 2 (if x is even). Return the distance of target when it is popped, or -1 if the heap empties first.
editorial: Because operations have different prices, breadth-first search (which minimises the number of operations) is wrong; for example a long run of cheap additions may beat one expensive doubling. The state is only the current number, so the state graph has limit + 1 vertices and at most three outgoing edges each: this is shortest path with positive weights, the textbook use case for Dijkstra.

Maintain dist[x] for all numbers in range, a min-heap of (price, x), and expand a number by generating its neighbours. The first pop of target gives the minimum price. The limit also bounds how far a detour can go (for example doubling past the target and then halving back), so no extra argument is needed to stop the search.

Time O(limit log limit), space O(limit). Note that doubling 0 or halving 0 just returns to 0 and never improves anything, so no special case is required. If target is smaller than start it can only be reached by halving steps, so the answer may be -1.
time: O(L log L) with L = limit
